nameStory: This paradise jumping spider gets its species name 'viridipes' from Latin, meaning 'green feet' - a perfect description of its most striking feature. The males sport brilliant green front legs that they wave like colorful flags during their courtship dances, making them look like tiny performers on nature's stage.
description: The Green-legged Paradise Jumping Spider is a small, brownish-black jumping spider that reaches about 5.5 millimeters long - roughly the size of a pencil eraser. What makes this spider truly special are the males' vibrant green front legs, which they use in elaborate courtship displays. Like all jumping spiders, they have excellent vision and hunt by stalking and pouncing on prey rather than building webs. You'll find them throughout eastern North America, including much of New England.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Males have striking bright green front legs that catch the light like tiny emeralds - this is the easiest way to identify this species

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, stocky build typical of jumping spiders with a relatively flat, rectangular cephalothorax (front body section) that feels firm to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider at about 5.5mm long - you could fit two of them on your thumbnail with room to spare

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent front-facing eyes arranged in a rectangular pattern that give them an almost curious, alert expression

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Males perform distinctive courtship dances, lifting and waving their green front legs while approaching females - watch for this jerky, stop-and-start movement

habitat: Look for these spiders in sunny, open areas like meadows, field edges, and woodland clearings where they hunt on low vegetation and leaf litter. They prefer areas with mixed grasses and wildflowers where they can easily spot flying insects from their perches. You might also find them on fence posts, garden plants, or sunlit rocks where they bask and watch for prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, with males beginning their courtship displays in late spring when you're most likely to spot those flashy green legs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both hunting and mating behaviors are most visible - the best time to observe their characteristic jumping and dancing.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues but slows as temperatures drop, with spiders seeking sheltered spots for overwintering.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected locations under bark, rocks, or leaf litter, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Male Green-legged Paradise Jumping Spiders are some of nature's most dedicated dancers - they'll perform their green-leg-waving courtship routine for up to 45 minutes straight, essentially doing an elaborate spider ballet to win over a female who might eat them if she's not impressed!
confusionNotes: Other jumping spiders in New England lack the distinctive bright green front legs of male viridipes, making this species fairly easy to identify when males are present. Females and juveniles are trickier, appearing as typical small brown jumping spiders, but their habitat preferences and the stockier build can help distinguish them.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'paradise' in paradise jumping spiders refers to their often spectacular courtship displays and colorful ornaments, reminiscent of birds-of-paradise. Don't let the name fool you into thinking they're tropical - many paradise jumping spiders are perfectly adapted to temperate climates.
compareHints: Among its paradise jumping spider relatives, viridipes is the only species with bright green front legs in males, making it relatively easy to distinguish from other Habronattus species. The Boreal Paradise Spider (H. borealis) is darker overall and lacks green coloration, while other relatives in the genus tend to have different color patterns or geographic ranges that don't overlap as much with New England.
